summary: This short document updates RFC 8428, Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML), by specifying independently selectable SenML Features and mapping them to SenML version numbers.

plainLanguage.summary: Sensor message formats grow new abilities over time. This document explains how to pick which abilities a message uses and how they connect to version numbers.

questions: what is the senml version number
subtitle: SenML's single version number becomes a bitmap, so independent optional features can be added without a strict version ladder.

tldr.problem: SenML had a version number set to 10 but no rule for how to evolve it, and a plain incrementing number would imply that every newer version understands everything older.
tldr.mechanism: Each SenML Feature gets a feature code below 53, and the version number (the bver field) is the sum of 2 to the power of each present feature code.
tldr.outcome: Features can be added independently. Version 10 stays the base, and Secondary Units (code 4) gives version 26. An implementation must check the bits, not just compare numbers.

today: RFC 9100 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8428. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why SenML Needs Features
sections.content:
SenML (Sensor Measurement Lists, RFC 8428) carries a version number that is initially set to 10, with no further guidance on how different version numbers should be used.

A version number normally assumes steady, incremental growth as a format gains features. For SenML the expectation is different: independently selectable capability features will be added to the basic specification that version 10 indicates. To support that model, this document reuses the single version number of a pack of SenML records as a bitmap. The bitmap shows which features a recipient must have implemented to process the pack.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a new version just means 'more stuff', in order. Here the designers expect separate add-ons instead, so the version number is turned into a list of which add-ons are used.

sections.title: Feature Codes and the Version Bitmap
sections.content:
Each SenML Feature has a feature name (a text string) and a feature code (an unsigned integer less than 53). A pack's version is built from the set of features it uses.

The version number, carried in the bver field, is the sum of two to the power of the feature code, taken over every feature that is present. In C-like languages, 2 to the power of fc can be written as 1 << fc.

The limit of 53 comes from the integer range that all SenML representations can carry: practical JSON limits this to 2^53-1. Feature codes 4 to 52 are available, one is taken by Secondary Units, and that leaves 48 for allocation. The RFC suggests allocating roughly two feature codes per year or fewer over a lifetime of several decades.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ability gets its own switch position. Add up the value of every switch that is on and you get one number that tells the whole story.

sections.title: Versions Are No Longer Totally Ordered
sections.content:
The last paragraph of Section 4.4 of RFC 8428 can be read to mean that an implementation understanding version n also understands all versions below n. This RFC says that, whatever was true before version 10, it is not true now.

Any pack that sets feature bits beyond the first four has a version number greater than 10, so the existing RFC 8428 rule keeps it from being mistaken for something a version 10 implementation can handle.

An implementation that supports feature bits beyond the first four must compare the bitmap bit by bit and check that every indicated feature is understood before using the pack. For example, an implementation with basic SenML plus a future feature code 5 accepts version 42, but cannot work with a pack indicating version 26 (the base plus feature code 4). If it requires feature code 5 without being backwards compatible, it accepts 42 but not 10.

Version numbers do not simply increase linearly. The RFC itself notes this as a potential for surprise.
sections.plainLanguage: A bigger number does not mean 'knows more'. You have to check which specific switches the message needs and see whether you have all of them.

sections.title: The Reserved Features and Secondary Units
sections.content:
For version 10 as defined in RFC 8428, feature codes 0 to 3 are already in use. Reserved1 (1) and Reserved3 (3) are always present, and Reserved0 (0) and Reserved2 (2) are always absent. The four least significant bits are therefore 0b1010, which is the number 10. These four codes must not be given more specific meaning except in a specification that updates this one.

The first real feature is Secondary Units (code 4). It means that secondary unit names from RFC 8798 MAY be used in the u field of SenML records, in addition to the primary unit names already allowed by RFC 8428. Its most basic use sets the version number to 26, which is 10 plus 2^4.

Less generally applicable features can instead be communicated through fields whose names end with the _ character (must-understand fields), described in Section 4.4 of RFC 8428.
sections.plainLanguage: The first four switches are already set and locked so old messages still read as 10. The first new switch lets a message use extra kinds of measurement units.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8428 apply. Giving structure to the interpretation of the version number poses no additional security considerations, except for some potential for surprise that version numbers do not simply increase linearly.

The RFC also warns about interoperability: with dozens of individually selectable extensions, there may be too many variants supported by different implementations. It therefore remains desirable to batch up extensions that are expected to be supported together into one feature bit.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing new to worry about for safety. The only trap is that the numbers do not go up in a neat line.

sections.title: The SenML Features Registry
sections.content:
IANA has created a "SenML Features" subregistry in the Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) registry. The registration policy is Specification Required, and the columns are Feature Code, Feature Name and Reference.

The designated expert is asked to make sure feature names work as identifiers in most programming languages (after lowercasing and replacing blank space with underscores or hyphens) and are distinct in that form. Because only 48 codes are left, the expert is told to be frugal and keep codes for features likely to be useful to non-trivial subsets of the SenML ecosystem. As an example the RFC says the expert could aim at not allocating more than 10% of the remaining set per year.

Where a feature code is specified in a different document from the feature itself, as with code 4, both references should be listed.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of switches. The person in charge of the list hands out new switches slowly so they do not run out.
